strengths: Soundness: The central reduction is mathematically coherent. MaxSim decomposes over query tokens, and the linear output layer makes each learned document row a latent vector, turning candidate generation into maximum-inner-product search followed by exact MaxSim reranking.

Significance: Efficient multi-vector retrieval is an important systems problem. LEMUR reports substantial practical gains: Table 2 shows roughly 5–11× higher QPS than the strongest baseline at at least 80% recall on the larger ColBERTv2 benchmarks.

Evaluation breadth is unusually good for this topic: six BEIR corpora, five text embedding models, two visual-document models, and several strong baselines. Results on non-ColBERTv2 and visual embeddings usefully reveal weaknesses that ColBERTv2-only evaluations can hide.

The ablations support important design choices: Figures 2–3 examine latent dimension and approximate versus exact latent-space search, while Appendix D tests three sources of training embeddings and shows that actual queries help but are not essential.

Presentation is clear and concise. The supervised-learning formulation, scalable fitting procedure, and retrieval pipeline are easy to follow, and the appendix supplies the main training hyperparameters.

Originality is meaningful, though not radical: learning a corpus-specific low-dimensional factorization of token-to-document MaxSim scores and reinterpreting output weights as ANN vectors is a simple and effective alternative to data-oblivious encodings such as MUVERA.
The work uses established public retrieval benchmarks and presents no apparent material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence focuses almost exclusively on query throughput versus recall of exact MaxSim neighbors. It reports neither index size nor peak memory, despite storing a 2048-dimensional vector for every document in addition to representations needed for reranking. Index construction time, feature-encoder training time, and update costs are also absent. These omissions prevent a complete systems comparison and weaken the paper’s scalability claims.

The manuscript frequently frames QPS measured by parallelizing queries over all 40 CPU cores as latency. Throughput does not establish single-query or tail latency; batching, warm-up, repeated-run variance, and p50/p95 latency are not reported. No confidence intervals or run-to-run variability are shown.

Baseline tuning is not sufficiently transparent for the magnitude of the claimed gains. The exact grids for candidate counts, ef_search, and clusters probed are omitted; most index hyperparameters are fixed to recommended values while DESSERT receives a limited grid search. Software versions, compiler settings, random seeds, and model revisions are also missing.

Hyperparameters are selected and Pareto frontiers are reported using recall on the same benchmark query sets used for evaluation. This is conventional in ANN benchmarking but permits test-set tuning; a held-out tuning split or robustness analysis would make the comparisons more convincing.
The visual evaluation pools five ViDoRe datasets into only 100 queries and reports no per-dataset results or uncertainty, so the evidence for multimodal generality is limited.

The method is corpus-specific: document vectors are learned output weights, and the feature encoder is pretrained against sampled corpus documents. Although per-document OLS fitting permits additions after the encoder is fixed, the paper does not study corpus evolution, distribution shift, deletion/update behavior, or when the shared feature encoder must be retrained.

There is no theoretical or empirical characterization of approximation error beyond recall curves. In particular, the paper does not analyze which queries or documents fail, sensitivity to the sampled 8,192 output documents and 100,000 training tokens, or variability across sampling seeds.

Reproducibility is only moderate. Table 3 helps, but the stated open-source URL is absent in the manuscript, preprocessing details are sparse, and the missing timing/memory and search-grid information would make exact reproduction difficult.

The limitations discussion is too narrow: it mentions low-precision compression but not the large learned index, training/indexing overhead, corpus specificity, test-set tuning, throughput-versus-latency distinction, or the small visual-query evaluation. These are material limitations, although they do not invalidate the core result.

strengths: The manuscript presents a clear and technically plausible reduction: it learns a token feature map whose pooled query representation is scored against corpus-specific output weights, thereby converting MaxSim candidate generation into conventional maximum-inner-product search. The algebra in Sections 3–4 is straightforward and internally consistent. The empirical gains are substantial: Table 2 reports roughly 5–11× higher throughput than the strongest baseline at at least 80% Recall@100 on the six ColBERTv2/BEIR datasets, and the full recall–throughput curves generally favor LEMUR.

Evaluation spans six text datasets, five text embedding models, two visual-document models, and several million-document corpora. This is considerably broader than an evaluation confined to ColBERTv2.

The comparisons partially control implementation effects by placing both LEMUR and MUVERA behind the same Glass index and MaxSim reranker. Ablations examine latent dimension, approximate versus exact search, k=10 versus k=100, and three sources of training embeddings.
The idea is simple but useful and reasonably original: unlike data-oblivious fixed-dimensional encodings, the representation is directly fitted to corpus-specific token-to-document MaxSim targets.

The paper is well organized, supplies core training hyperparameters, and includes an honest—though incomplete—limitations paragraph. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent for this retrieval-systems work.
weaknesses: The headline latency claim is not directly established. Experiments parallelize queries over all 40 CPU cores and report aggregate QPS, which measures throughput rather than single-query or tail latency. The abstract and discussion repeatedly claim lower latency and an order-of-magnitude speedup, but no per-query latency distribution, batch size, warm-up protocol, or p50/p95/p99 latency is reported.

The efficiency evaluation omits major costs introduced by the method. LEMUR stores one 2048-dimensional learned vector per document, requires corpus-dependent training and per-document OLS fitting, and still retains original multi-vectors for reranking. The paper reports neither peak/index memory nor total index-construction time, training time, model size, or update cost on each corpus. Consequently, it does not establish overall system efficiency or scalability despite making those central claims.

Hyperparameter selection appears to use the evaluation queries themselves: the authors grid-search query-time parameters and report the Pareto-optimal configurations on each benchmark, without a validation split or a fixed tuning protocol. This gives oracle test-set operating curves and can overstate practical performance, even if the procedure is applied to all methods.

Baseline tuning is under-specified and potentially uneven. Most index parameters are fixed to recommended values, DESSERT alone receives an explicit grid search, and the full query grids, stopping criteria, software versions, compiler flags, thread settings, and baseline-specific tuning budgets are absent. Comparisons across official C++, Rust, PyTorch, and custom C++ components therefore remain difficult to audit.

The evaluation reports no repetitions, random seeds, confidence intervals, or sensitivity to sampled training tokens/documents. This is especially problematic for ViDoRe, which contains only 100 pooled test queries, and for a learned method whose training set is randomly sampled.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper says the code is available but provides no visible repository URL in the manuscript, and several essential implementation details are missing, including the precise OLS solver and regularization, numerical precision, scalar-quantization settings, exact search grids, preprocessing, and timing methodology.

The limitations discussion focuses almost exclusively on low-precision compression. It does not acknowledge the corpus-specific fitting requirement, memory/build-time tradeoffs, dynamic-corpus behavior, test-set tuning, small visual-query sample, or the distinction between throughput and latency.

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional: the central construction is a supervised low-rank factorization of document-wise MaxSim target functions followed by standard MIPS. The paper provides neither approximation/generalization guarantees nor a deeper analysis of when this corpus-specific factorization should succeed or fail.

Overall, the method and results are promising enough for a weak accept, but the evidence supports a strong throughput result more convincingly than the broader claims of low-latency, memory-efficient retrieval at scale. Reporting end-to-end resource costs, latency distributions, validation-based tuning, and repeated measurements would be needed for a confident accept.

strengths: Soundness: The central reduction is technically coherent: the per-document MaxSim contribution is learned with a shared feature encoder and linear document-specific outputs, making the pooled query representation compatible with maximum-inner-product search followed by exact MaxSim reranking.

Evaluation: The study is unusually broad for this problem, covering six BEIR corpora, five text embedding models, two visual-document models, and four established baselines. LEMUR consistently improves the recall-throughput frontier; at 80% recall on ColBERTv2, Table 2 reports 5–11× higher QPS than the strongest baseline.

Significance: Efficient multi-vector retrieval is an important practical bottleneck. Producing standard single-vector representations permits reuse of mature ANNS infrastructure and could materially simplify deployment.

Originality: Learning a corpus-specific latent factorization of token-to-document MaxSim contributions is a simple but insightful alternative to token-level pruning and data-oblivious fixed-dimensional encodings.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript is clear and well organized, provides pseudomathematical specification of the method, hardware details, training hyperparameters, baseline implementations, and useful ablations over latent dimension, ANNS approximation, and training-data choice. The document-encoder experiment is particularly valuable: it shows that the gains persist even when LEMUR is trained without additional queries or access to the query encoder, reducing concern that the main results depend entirely on privileged training data.

Ethics: The work raises no evident concerns involving sensitive data, human subjects, or harmful applications, and its limitations discussion appropriately acknowledges compression-related constraints.
weaknesses: Soundness and significance: The evaluation reports retrieval QPS but omits peak/index memory, index-construction time, model-training time, and storage overhead. These are central to the efficiency claim because LEMUR stores a 2048-dimensional learned vector for every document plus an HNSW graph, while its motivation explicitly emphasizes memory and scalability.

The claimed order-of-magnitude speedup is not universal. The visual-retrieval curves show a substantially narrower advantage, particularly at high recall, and some ColBERTv2 curves converge toward competing methods near maximum recall. The headline claim should be qualified by operating regime.

Experimental uncertainty is not characterized: there are no repeated runs, error bars, latency distributions, or discussion of warm-up and cache conditions. Small throughput differences therefore cannot be interpreted reliably, although the largest reported gaps are unlikely to be explained by noise.

Baseline fairness is reasonable but not fully established. LEMUR and MUVERA share Glass and the same reranker, whereas other methods use separate implementations and mostly author-recommended fixed index settings; only DESSERT receives an index-parameter grid search. Broader baseline index tuning would make the systems comparison more conclusive.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful hyperparameter table: the manuscript does not give the exact query-parameter grids, random seeds, software versions or commits, preprocessing details, or the identities of the five pooled ViDoRe subsets. The visible manuscript also says that code is available but provides no link.

The limitations section is too narrow. It discusses low-precision compression but not corpus-specific training, the cost of rebuilding or maintaining the learned index under substantial corpus updates, hardware dependence of QPS, or the large per-document latent index. These issues limit the strength of the deployment claims.

strengths: The paper presents a simple and original corpus-specific reduction of MaxSim search to single-vector maximum-inner-product search: a shared nonlinear feature map approximates token-level support functions, while the learned output-layer rows become document vectors. The formulation is technically coherent, and the exact MaxSim reranking stage preserves a clear accuracy-control mechanism.

The empirical evidence is broad and consistently favorable. Evaluation covers eight BEIR datasets, several modern text embedding models, two visual-document models, and a long-query setting. On ColBERTv2, LEMUR reports 5–16× higher QPS than the best baseline at at least 80% recall, with similarly strong Pareto curves beyond ColBERTv2.

The comparisons include strong and relevant systems (MUVERA, PLAID, DESSERT, and IGP). Reusing the same ANNS library and exact reranking implementation for LEMUR and MUVERA improves the fairness of the most direct comparison.

The ablations are informative: the paper studies latent dimensionality, candidate recall, score correlation, different training-data sources, and random hidden features. These results support the claim that the method is robust and that learned features provide more accurate, lower-dimensional encodings than MUVERA's fixed encodings.

The contribution is practically significant. It can leverage established single-vector ANNS infrastructure, supports incremental document insertion after fixing the feature encoder, and substantially improves retrieval throughput across modalities. The exposition and algorithms are generally clear, and hyperparameters and hardware are documented.

The limitations discussion appropriately acknowledges incremental-index construction and low-precision compression as unresolved issues. The work raises no evident material ethical concern; its impact statement is brief but proportionate to an efficiency-focused retrieval contribution.
weaknesses: The systems evaluation does not report peak or end-to-end memory consumption, despite making scalability and memory-efficiency arguments. LEMUR stores a 2048-dimensional vector per document, an ANNS graph, and the original multi-vector representations required for reranking; quantified comparisons with every baseline are needed to establish the full operational tradeoff.

Timing evidence comes from one CPU platform and is reported without repeated-run variability, warm-up methodology, batching details, or latency percentiles. Because queries are parallelized across all 40 cores, QPS primarily measures throughput and does not by itself substantiate interactive per-query latency claims.

Baseline comparisons mix official implementations in different languages and optimization states. Although the MUVERA comparison is especially well controlled, the large advantages over PLAID, DESSERT, and IGP could partly reflect implementation effects. Cross-hardware experiments or profiling by pipeline stage would strengthen the central performance claim.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the submitted manuscript: the stated code link is blank, and the precise query-time grid values for ef_search, candidate counts, and numbers of probed clusters are not listed. Random seeds, timing protocol, preprocessing details, and exact model checkpoints should also be consolidated.

Only LEMUR's indexing time is reported. Index construction time, index size, and update cost are not compared systematically against the baselines, so the claim of superior indexing scalability is less well supported than the query-time claim.

The universal-approximation theorem is correct but weak: its required dimension may depend on the corpus size, and it supplies neither a finite-dimensional error bound nor a ranking/recall guarantee. Thus it offers limited explanation for why a fixed dimension of 2048 works at scale; the empirical results, rather than the theorem, carry the soundness of the method.

The downstream relevance-quality check is less comprehensive than the MaxSim-recall evaluation: the nDCG table omits MS MARCO, and several datasets have only 49–100 test queries. Confidence intervals or per-query significance tests would help establish the robustness of the reported retrieval-quality preservation.

strengths: Soundness: The core reduction is algebraically clean: MaxSim decomposes over query tokens, a shared feature map plus document-specific linear heads yields inner-product query/document representations, and exact MaxSim reranking restores precision within the candidate set.

Significance: If the reported results reproduce, the gains are practically meaningful. At at least 80% Recall@100, LEMUR reports roughly 5–16× higher QPS than the strongest baseline across eight BEIR collections.

Evaluation breadth: The experiments cover eight text datasets, several recent late-interaction text encoders, two visual-document encoders, long queries, two retrieval cutoffs, and multiple training-data choices. This is considerably broader than a ColBERTv2-only evaluation.

Presentation: The paper is well organized, and the method, indexing procedure, query pipeline, and main hyperparameters are explained clearly. The limitations discussion appropriately acknowledges incremental indexing and compression issues.

Originality: Learning a corpus-specific single-vector reduction through multi-output regression is a simple but useful departure from data-oblivious fixed-dimensional encodings. The random-feature experiment also provides an interesting insight into why the approach may work.
weaknesses: Reproducibility and computational soundness are the decisive concern. The stated workload appears difficult to reconcile with the reported CPU indexing times. For MSMARCO, forming all OLS heads as written entails a dense operation on approximately 8.8M documents, 16,384 samples, and 2,048 features—about 2.95e14 multiply-accumulates—before accounting for constructing the MaxSim targets. Likewise, 100 epochs over 100,000 examples with an 8,192-output layer is extremely expensive. The paper reports only 70 and 20 minutes, respectively, on two Xeon 6230 CPUs, without explaining an algorithmic shortcut, batching scheme, precision, or hardware utilization that makes these figures plausible.

The headline claim is about latency, but the experiments report aggregate QPS while explicitly parallelizing queries across all 40 CPU cores. This measures saturated throughput rather than single-query latency and provides no median or tail latency. The evidence therefore does not directly support the repeated low-latency and online-serving claims.

The system comparison omits important resource dimensions. There are no measured peak RAM, index size, retained token-storage cost, energy, or baseline indexing times. A 2,048-dimensional vector for every one of 8.8M documents is already about 72 GB in float32 before the graph and exact-reranking representations. Consequently, claims of better scalability and reduced memory are established only indirectly and mainly relative to MUVERA's dimensionality.

Baseline fairness is insufficiently documented. LEMUR and MUVERA vary two query parameters, DESSERT receives a small grid search, while most index parameters are fixed to recommended settings; the actual search grids are not given. EMVB is discussed but not evaluated, and WARP is excluded without an empirical comparison. No confidence intervals or repeated-run variability are reported, including for datasets with only 49–100 queries.

The universal-approximation result is mathematically weak evidence for the practical method. It assumes universality, permits the hidden dimension to depend on the entire finite corpus and desired error, gives no usable dimension or sample-complexity bound, and says nothing about ranking recall under approximate nearest-neighbor search. It also does not justify the specific layer-normalized, one-hidden-layer architecture used experimentally.

Important experimental details remain absent: random seeds, numerical precision, exact ranges for ef-search, candidate count, probes, and reranking count, timing methodology and warm-up, preprocessing details, and model/library versions. The abstract promises code but the manuscript contains no usable code location. These omissions are especially material given the unexplained indexing-time discrepancy.

End-task validation is incomplete. Most conclusions use recall relative to exact MaxSim rather than relevance judgments. The nDCG appendix covers only seven of the eight BEIR datasets, omitting MSMARCO, and gives thresholded QPS rather than full quality–efficiency curves; no relevance-based results are supplied for the visual benchmark.

Ethics and limitations: The limitations section is useful, but the impact statement dismisses direct societal impact too quickly. Retrieval systems can inherit encoder and corpus biases and can affect access to information; dataset licensing, privacy, and deployment failure modes are not discussed. These are secondary concerns rather than the main reason for rejection.

strengths: Soundness: The central construction is technically coherent. Writing each document’s token-level MaxSim contribution as a support function, approximating all such functions with a shared nonlinear feature map and document-specific linear outputs, and pooling query-token features yields a valid reduction to maximum-inner-product search followed by exact MaxSim reranking.

Evidence: The evaluation is unusually broad for a retrieval-systems paper: eight BEIR corpora, multiple modern text encoders, two visual-document encoders, long queries, k=10 and k=100 settings, and comparisons with MUVERA, IGP, DESSERT, and PLAID. On ColBERTv2, LEMUR reaches at least 80% recall at 5–16x the QPS of the strongest reported baseline, with consistent Pareto-front improvements across datasets.

Significance: Making late-interaction retrieval compatible with standard single-vector ANNS infrastructure is practically valuable. The reported 1024–2048-dimensional learned representations are substantially more accurate than MUVERA’s 10240-dimensional FDEs, addressing both latency and integration complexity.

Originality: The combination of corpus-specific multi-output regression, a shared learned feature expansion, closed-form per-document output fitting, and interpreting the output weights as document vectors is simple but insightful. It provides a useful learned alternative to data-oblivious reductions and token-level pruning.

The ablations substantiate several design choices: latent dimension, MaxSim correlation, training-data source, random versus trained hidden features, and robustness to query length. The document-encoder-only experiment is especially useful because it shows that the method need not rely on external queries.

Presentation is clear and economical. The manuscript gives explicit algorithms for indexing and querying, a correct universal-approximation statement, concrete training hyperparameters, and informative recall–throughput curves. The limitations discussion candidly identifies incremental indexing and aggressive compression as open problems. weaknesses: The systems evaluation does not report peak memory, final index sizes, or a matched comparison of index-construction costs. This is important because LEMUR stores one 2048-dimensional vector per document, an HNSW-style graph, and the original multi-vector representations needed for reranking; at 8.8 million documents, these resources can be substantial.

The throughput methodology is underspecified: the paper does not state the number of timing repetitions, warm-up procedure, variance, thread affinity, batching, or whether preprocessing and all query-side feature computation are included. Results are confined to one 40-core CPU platform, and the suggested GPU applicability is not experimentally demonstrated.

Reproducibility is only moderate. Training hyperparameters and high-level baseline settings are documented, but the query-time search grids and several low-level implementation choices are absent. The abstract says that code is available but provides no visible URL in the supplied manuscript, so the custom C++ reranker and complete benchmarking pipeline cannot presently be inspected.

The universal-approximation result is mathematically correct but weak: it supplies neither a finite-width bound nor a ranking/recall guarantee, and its required width may depend strongly on corpus size and geometry. The empirical results, rather than this theorem, carry the paper’s central claims.

The broad model evaluation is mostly conducted on small corpora such as Quora, SCIDOCS, and ViDoRe; large-scale experiments use ColBERTv2. Consequently, robustness to newer embedding models at multi-million-document scale remains unverified.

Baseline tuning could be more convincing. Most index parameters are fixed to recommended values, while query parameters are swept; only DESSERT receives a small index grid. Reporting each baseline’s memory/indexing budget and either matched-budget tuning or sensitivity analyses would better establish fairness.

The retrieval-quality table omits MS MARCO despite the main evaluation using eight BEIR datasets, and the paper reports no uncertainty for QPS or retrieval metrics. The impact statement is also overly categorical: efficient retrieval has limited direct risk, but deployed retrieval systems can inherit representational and content biases from their encoders and corpora. These are limitations rather than acceptance-blocking ethical concerns.
